passage:
I'm Vidya, and last week I sighed the loudest in maths. Jomon was stuck on the same fraction sum for ages, tapping his pencil and staring. I finished mine, then whispered, "It's so easy!" and rolled my eyes. Jomon's ears went red.
Our teacher walked over to Jomon and didn't sigh. She drew the sum as a chocolate bar and waited while he tried. When Jomon got it, she just nodded, as if it hadn't taken long at all.
My face went warm. The next day I said, "Do you want to see how I did it?" and Jomon did.

qa.q: What sum was Jomon stuck on?
qa.a: The same fraction sum, for ages.

qa.q: What did Vidya feel when watching the teacher help Jomon?
qa.a: Vidya felt embarrassed. The warm face shows that Vidya realised the sighs and eye-rolling were unkind.

qa.q: What choice did Vidya make the next day?
qa.a: Vidya offered to show Jomon how Vidya had done the sum, instead of sighing.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt when Vidya whispered 'It's so easy!'?
qa.a: Embarrassed and hurt, since Jomon's ears went red.

grounding: A quick child sighs at a slower classmate's struggle and learns patience by watching a teacher deal with slowness kindly.

passage:
Note from Sabina, class 4 teacher. During fractions today Sudha finished early, then sighed loudly each time Ravi paused over his sum, and finally muttered, "Hurry up." Ravi stopped writing and looked at his desk. I did not scold her in front of the class.
At break I asked Sudha to help me draw a number line for everyone, and told her it took me a long time to learn it too. She was quiet. Later I overheard her say to Ravi, "You can borrow my ruler."
I will pair them on Thursday and keep modelling patience. Sudha is quick, but she has not yet seen that people move at different speeds.

qa.q: What did Sudha mutter to Ravi?
qa.a: 'Hurry up.'

qa.q: How might Ravi have felt when Sudha sighed and muttered?
qa.a: Embarrassed and pressured. He stopped writing and looked at his desk.

qa.q: What did Sabina do instead of scolding Sudha in front of the class?
qa.a: Sabina asked Sudha to help draw a number line and said it took Sabina a long time to learn it too, showing that pace differs.

qa.q: What does Sabina think Sudha has not yet understood?
qa.a: That people move at different speeds. Sudha is quick but has not yet seen how slower classmates feel.

grounding: A quick child sighs at a slower classmate's struggle, and an adult models patience.

passage:
In the Class 4 maths period at their Kolkata school, Afreen finished the fractions sheet in five minutes. Beside her, Farhan was still on question two, rubbing out the same answer. Afreen sighed loudly and drummed her pencil. "It's so easy," she muttered.
Farhan's ears went pink.
Ms Ghosh came over and knelt by Farhan's desk. She didn't sigh. "Show me how you're thinking about it." She drew a pizza, cut it into quarters, and waited while Farhan counted slices. He got it. Then he got the next one too.
Afreen watched. Ms Ghosh had waited so long, and Farhan's face had changed from tight to bright.
When he got stuck on question five, Afreen didn't sigh. She drew a small pizza in the corner of his sheet.

qa.q: What did Ms Ghosh draw?
qa.a: A pizza cut into quarters.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel when Afreen sighed?
qa.a: Farhan felt embarrassed, his ears going pink.

qa.q: What did Afreen learn from watching Ms Ghosh?
qa.a: That waiting patiently and showing a picture helps, so she drew a pizza for Farhan instead of sighing.

qa.q: What might Ms Ghosh have noticed about Afreen?
qa.a: Ms Ghosh probably noticed Afreen's impatience and chose to show a kinder way rather than lecture.

grounding: Shows a quick child sighing at a slower classmate and learning patience by watching a teacher handle slowness kindly.

passage:
"Just hit it, Jeevan! It's not hard!"
Jeevan swung and missed again. The tennis ball bounced off the wall. "Sorry."
Kunal threw up his hands. "That's six times."
Their grandfather looked up from his newspaper on the step. "Kunal. How many times did I bowl to you before you hit one, two summers ago?"
Kunal went quiet. "A lot."
"Forty-one. I counted." Dadaji folded the paper and came over. "Jeevan, keep your eyes on the ball, not the bat. Take your time." He tossed it gently. Jeevan missed. Dadaji tossed again, just as gently. On the fourth, Jeevan hit it and whooped.
Kunal picked up the ball. "Okay. My turn to bowl. Slow ones."

qa.q: How many times did Dadaji bowl before Kunal first hit one?
qa.a: Forty-one.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling after Dadaji's question?
qa.a: Kunal felt a bit embarrassed and went quiet, remembering how long it took him too.

qa.q: What did Kunal learn from watching Dadaji?
qa.a: That gentle, repeated tosses and one calm tip help a slower learner, so he offered to bowl slow ones.

qa.q: What was the practice like for Jeevan before Dadaji stepped in?
qa.a: Jeevan felt pressured and apologetic, saying "Sorry" after each miss.

grounding: Shows a quick child losing patience with a slower player and learning patience from an elder's kind handling.

passage:
When I was ten, I was the fastest reader in my class, and I hated reading-aloud time because Anjali was so slow. She'd stop at every long word, and I'd roll my eyes and finish the sentence for her.
One day my Ammi came to help in class. She sat next to Anjali and waited, really waited, while Anjali sounded out "e-le-phant". Ammi just smiled and said, "Good, keep going." Anjali read the whole page.
At home I asked Ammi why she waited so long. She said, "Everyone walks at their own speed. I waited for you once too, when you couldn't tie your laces." I'm Zeenat, and I stopped finishing Anjali's sentences after that.

qa.q: Which word did Anjali sound out?
qa.a: Elephant, sounded out as e-le-phant.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel during reading-aloud time?
qa.a: Zeenat felt impatient and annoyed, rolling eyes and finishing Anjali's sentences.

qa.q: What changed Zeenat's behaviour?
qa.a: Watching Ammi wait kindly for Anjali, and hearing that Ammi had once waited for Zeenat too.

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt when Ammi waited for her?
qa.a: Anjali probably felt encouraged and less rushed, and read the whole page.

grounding: Shows a quick child impatient with a slower reader, learning patience from watching a parent wait kindly.

passage:
Class 4B observation note, Thursday, maths period.
During the pair task on carrying over, Kashish finished all six sums in four minutes. Sangeeta was still on the second one, rubbing out the same digit again and again. Kashish sighed loudly twice and said, "It's easy, just do it." Sangeeta's ears went red and she stopped writing.
I sat down with them and worked the second sum slowly with Sangeeta, saying each step out loud and waiting whenever she paused. Kashish watched the whole time. On the fourth sum, Kashish started to speak, stopped, and asked instead, "Do you want me to show you the tens part?"
Next step: pair them again on Monday, with Kashish as the explainer, not the checker.

qa.q: How long did Kashish take to finish all six sums?
qa.a: Kashish finished all six sums in four minutes.

qa.q: Why do you think Kashish stopped and asked a question on the fourth sum?
qa.a: After watching the teacher wait calmly, Kashish seemed less impatient and more curious about where Sangeeta was stuck, and wanted to help instead of hurry her.

qa.q: What could Kashish try the next time a partner works more slowly?
qa.a: Kashish could wait quietly for a moment and then ask which step feels tricky, the way the teacher did, instead of sighing.

qa.q: What was it like for Sangeeta when Kashish sighed and said it was easy?
qa.a: It likely made her feel slow and embarrassed; her ears went red and she stopped writing.

grounding: Shows a quick child's impatience with a slower classmate softening after watching a teacher handle slowness kindly.
